name: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
title: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
answer: Text to video with a focus on physics and continuity covers systems that turn a written prompt into a moving image sequence while keeping the result physically plausible and visually consistent from frame to frame. In cinematography and video synthesis this means the model must respect object permanence, consistent lighting and shadows, realistic mass and momentum, and cause and effect such as a ball bouncing rather than passing through a floor. Continuity also includes matching wardrobe, props, and background details across cuts and camera angles, and keeping motion smooth without sudden jumps or morphing. The scope extends to camera movement, depth of field, and shot composition described in the prompt.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on large clusters of graphics processing units or tensor processing units, both for training and for generating video. Training requires very high memory bandwidth and many hours of compute across distributed hardware, while inference for a short clip still needs a capable GPU with substantial video memory. Most production use is cloud based because local hardware rarely has enough capacity for high resolution or long sequences. The models are typically diffusion based or autoregressive transformer based, but the infrastructure is similar: fast interconnects, large storage for video datasets, and checkpointing for long training runs.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by training a model on pairs of text descriptions and video clips, often with additional conditioning on frame rate, camera motion, or depth. During generation the model starts from noise or a low resolution latent and iteratively refines it, guided by the text embedding, while temporal attention layers or 3D convolutions share information across frames. To improve physics and continuity, practitioners add optical flow estimates, depth maps, or physics simulator outputs as auxiliary signals during training, and may use a second pass to inpaint inconsistent regions or stabilize motion. The result is a sequence where each frame is generated with awareness of its neighbours rather than independently.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on training data provenance, likeness and voice misuse, and the spread of fabricated events. Many training sets include copyrighted video, and the legal status of learning from that material is unsettled in several jurisdictions. Continuity and physics failures can create misleading footage that looks real enough to deceive, so provenance labels, watermarking, and disclosure requirements are becoming common practice even where not mandated. Creators should document the source material and model version, and avoid prompts that reproduce identifiable people or private spaces without consent. This page describes practice and does not give legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward longer, coherent shots with physically grounded motion and better control over camera and lighting. Researchers are combining video models with game engines, neural radiance fields, and physics simulators so that objects obey constraints instead of relying on statistical patterns alone. Expect improvements in object permanence across cuts, fewer morphing artefacts, and more reliable handling of liquids, cloth, and collisions. As the tools mature, continuity supervision may become a standard part of the editing workflow, with automatic detection of breaks in lighting, props, or motion.
